questions.text: The Settings endpoints need the app's CSRF check, but the confirm endpoint does not mention one. What stops another site from posting to confirm, and which cookie or token does the server rely on?

When the email matches an existing user, the pending record is created and the password form shown. What does the user see on that page, and does it say which Google account is being linked? Is anything else stored besides sub, user_id and next?
In the step 'Lowercased Google email equals users.email?' yes, what if that user has no password and no Google link? Can that happen, and what does the password form do for them?
What happens if someone who is already signed in uses GET /auth/google/start from the login page and completes it? Does start_session replace their current session?

The doc covers Redis being down at start and at the callback. What happens if Redis fails after the callback has consumed the attempt, for example when creating the pending record or at confirmation? Is the user told anything?
Where do the Google endpoints and signing keys come from, and are they fetched on every callback or cached? Does the 5s timeout cover the key fetch too?
questions.about: Server-to-server code exchange with PKCE verifier and client secret, 5s timeout

questions.text: On the Google login path, does start_session also reset failed_logins or touch locked_until? Also, the doc says it deletes 'any old sid row'. Which one: the sid cookie the browser sent?

answers.text: Confirm needs the app's normal CSRF token carried in the form, plus the g_pending cookie, which is SameSite=Lax so a cross-site POST does not send it. An attacker would also need the account password. I added this to the endpoint table and the flowchart; a missing or bad token goes to the error page.

The form names the matched account's email and says entering its password will link the Google account. That email equals the Google email (that is why it matched), so it needs no extra storage. The pending record holds only sub, target user_id and next. Added to the flowchart and the Redis table.

It should not happen: Google-created users (the only NULL-hash users) are always linked, and unlink is refused without a password, so a NULL-hash user without a link cannot exist. A NULL-hash user who is linked is refused earlier as having a different Google account. If it ever happened, check_password_with_lockout treats NULL as a wrong password, so the form never accepts and lockout applies. Added a line to the doc.

Yes, it is allowed. Per auth_flow.md, start_session deletes the sessions row named by the sid cookie the browser sent and creates a new one, so the old session is replaced even if the Google account belongs to a different user. Recorded as decision 7.

The attempt is already consumed, so the user sees an error page saying try again later, nothing is linked, no session starts, and they restart from login. A wrong-password count already written to PostgreSQL stays. If the pending record cannot be created, the same error page applies and nothing is written. Added a failure-table row.

Endpoints and signing keys come from Google's published discovery document and are cached in process memory; the 5s timeout applies to each outbound call to Google, including a key fetch. Cache lifetime is not specified, so I listed it as an open question: follow Google's cache headers and refetch on an unknown key ID.

No. start_session does not touch failed_logins or locked_until; POST /login resets failed_logins itself before calling it, and the Google path does not do that reset. It deletes the sessions row named by the sid cookie the browser sent, if any. Clarified in the doc.

questions.text: The confirm form is shown to someone who is not signed in. Where does its CSRF token come from and what is it tied to, given there is no session yet?
questions.about: POST /auth/google/confirm and Show password form naming the matched account's email

questions.text: The match compares the lowercased Google email to users.email. Is users.email always stored lowercased? If not, what happens when the cases differ?

answers.text: The confirm form is shown to a user with no session, so a session-bound CSRF token cannot be used. The form carries a confirm token that is an HMAC (server secret) of the pending ID. The server recomputes it from the g_pending cookie and compares. It is tied to that one pending record and expires with it. Together with the SameSite=Lax g_pending cookie and the need for the account password, this covers cross-site posting. I replaced the earlier 'app's normal CSRF token' wording for this endpoint. How the app's normal CSRF works for Settings is not in the files, so I listed it as an open question.

Yes. schema.sql says emails are stored lowercased and lowercased on every write, so users.email is always lowercase. Lowercasing the Google email makes the comparison exact and case never causes a miss. Added a line to the state section and a note on the match step.

questions.text: The callback checks that the g_bind cookie matches the record. Where does the record's bind value come from, and what exactly is compared (cookie value to the stored value)? What is this protecting against?
After a successful Google login, what does the user end up with in their browser, and is anything else changed in the database for them (for example last login or failed_logins)?

In the 'no match' branch, a new user is created with a NULL password. What is the user's only way to sign in afterwards, and what happens if they later use Sign in with Google from a different Google account with the same email?
questions.about: One DB transaction: insert user with password_hash NULL

questions.text: How does the confirm form get its confirm token and the g_pending cookie value? When the page is shown, is the token generated at that moment from the pending ID, and is the pending ID a random value?

When the password is wrong but the account is not yet locked, the form is shown again. Is there any limit other than the 5-failure lockout and the 10-minute TTL? And does the lockout from Google attempts also lock the user out of POST /login?
questions.about: Re-show form with generic wrong-password message

questions.text: Decision 1 says a locked linked user can still sign in with Google. But the confirm step refuses locked accounts. Why is the locked check there if the Google path skips it for linked users, and does it change that an attacker who knows the user's email could lock the account through the confirm form?
What does the user see on the 'Error page' and the 'Back to origin page' messages, and how does a message get shown on the login or Settings page after a redirect?
questions.about: Back to origin page with neutral message

answers.text: The bind value is a random value made at start. It is stored in the attempt record in Redis and set as the g_bind cookie. At the callback the cookie value must equal the stored value. It protects against login CSRF: someone feeding a victim's browser a callback URL from the attacker's own Google login. Added to the Cookies section and the flowchart.

The user ends up with a new sessions row and the sid cookie, and is redirected to the stored next or /home. start_session changes nothing else: no failed_logins reset, no locked_until change, and there is no last-login column in schema.sql. g_bind and g_pending are cleared. Added a line to the ending node.

A Google-created user can sign in only with Google until they set a password through the existing reset email (POST /forgot). If they use a different Google account with the same verified email, that sub is unlinked, the email matches their user, and that user already has a Google link, so it is refused as a different Google account. Added to the permanent state section.

The pending ID is random (32 random bytes, base64url), made when the pending record is created, and set as the g_pending cookie. The confirm token is the HMAC of that ID, computed each time the form is rendered and put in the form. Added to the flowchart node and the Cookies section.

No other limit exists: only the 5-failure lockout and the 10-minute window. Lockout is stored in users.failed_logins and locked_until, so failures at confirmation also lock the user out of POST /login, which is intended so the two paths cannot drift. Whether existing Redis rate limits on /login also cover confirm is not known; listed as an open question. Added as decision 9.

The locked check at confirmation is there because confirmation is password guessing, which lockout is meant to stop. Linked Google sign-in skips it because Google proves identity (decision 1). Reaching the confirm form needs a Google account with a verified email equal to the victim's, so it gives an attacker no new way to lock the account beyond what anyone who knows the email can already do at /login. Added to decision 9.

The error page shows the short message from the failure table with no technical detail, and the back-to-origin messages are shown once after the redirect. How the app implements a one-time message after a redirect (flash mechanism) and what its error page looks like are not in the existing files, so I do not know. Recorded as an open question; I suggested reusing the app's existing mechanism.

teachbacks.text:
1. Start. A user clicks "Sign in with Google" on the login page (GET /auth/google/start?next=..., anonymous) or "Link Google" in Account Settings (POST /settings/google/link). Settings needs a session and the normal CSRF check; with no session the user is redirected to login. The server creates an "attempt": random state, nonce, PKCE verifier and bind value, plus origin (login or settings), the validated relative `next`, and the signed-in user_id if origin is settings. It stores this in Redis at goog:attempt:STATE with a 600s TTL. It sets the g_bind cookie to the bind value and redirects the browser to Google. If Redis is down, the user sees an error page and nothing is written.

2. Google consent. The user sees Google's consent screen (scopes openid email profile). Google redirects the browser to the single registered URI, GET /auth/google/callback, carrying state and a code, or an error.

3. Callback gate. The server runs GETDEL on the attempt named by state. The record is deleted whatever happens next, so a callback is honoured only once. If state is missing, unknown, expired or used, the user gets an error page and nothing changes. Next the g_bind cookie must equal the bind value in the record. For a settings attempt, the signed-in user must also equal the record's user_id. A mismatch gives the error page.

4. Google error. If Google sent an `error` parameter (for example Cancel), the user goes back to the origin page (login keeps `next`) with a neutral "not completed" message. Nothing changes.

5. Code exchange and ID token check. The server makes a server-to-server exchange of the code, sending the PKCE verifier and client secret. It takes endpoints and keys from Google's discovery document, cached in memory, with a 5s timeout on each call. It validates the ID token (signature, iss, aud, exp, nonce, sub present). It reads sub, email and email_verified and discards all tokens. On any failure the user goes back to the origin page with "could not complete, try again", the reason is logged and nothing is written. The attempt is already consumed, so the user restarts.

6. Branch by origin. Login origin goes to step 7. Settings origin goes to step 12.

7. Login origin, lookup by sub. If sub is in user_google_accounts, the server signs that user in (step 11). It does not check lockout or email_verified for a linked sub. If sub is not linked, continue.

8. Unlinked sub. If email_verified is not true, the user goes back to login with a "Google email not verified, use email and password" message and nothing is created. If it is verified, the server compares the lowercased Google email to users.email.
   - No match: in one transaction, insert a user with password_hash NULL and email_verified_at now, and insert the user_google_accounts row. Then sign in (step 11). On a unique violation on email (a lost race), roll back and re-run the match once.
   - Match, and that user already has a Google link (necessarily a different sub): refuse and go back to login. No pending record is made.
   - Match, and that user has no Google link: go to step 9.

9. Pending link. The server makes a random pending ID (32 random bytes, base64url) and stores Redis goog:pending:ID with sub, target user_id and next, TTL 600s from the callback. It sets the g_pending cookie to the ID (scoped to /auth/google/confirm) and clears g_bind. It then shows a password form naming the matched account's email. The form carries a confirm token, an HMAC of the ID made with a server secret. A Redis failure here gives an error page and nothing is written.

10. Password confirmation (POST /auth/google/confirm, with password and confirm token). The server checks that the token matches the g_pending ID and that the cookie and Redis record exist. If not, the user gets an error page and must start again from login. Then:
   - If the target user's locked_until is in the future, or the wrong password causes lockout: delete the pending record, clear g_pending, and show "Account temporarily locked". The half-finished link is discarded.
   - Wrong password short of lockout: failed_logins goes up by 1 (at 5, locked_until becomes now plus 15 min and failed_logins resets to 0). The form is re-shown with the generic wrong-password message. The pending record stays with its original TTL. A NULL password_hash counts as a wrong password.
   - Correct password: failed_logins resets to 0. Redis GETDEL deletes the pending record. A nil result means a double submit and is treated as expired. The server then inserts the user_google_accounts row. A unique violation (linked meanwhile) refuses and links nothing. Otherwise it signs in (step 11).
   - The password check is the shared check_password_with_lockout, the same code /login uses. If Redis fails after the attempt was consumed, the user gets a "try again later" error page, nothing is linked and no session starts. Failed-password counts already saved in PostgreSQL stay.

11. Sign in. The server calls start_session(user_id), the same as a password login. It deletes the sessions row named by any sid cookie the browser sent, inserts a new sessions row, and sets the sid cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax). It changes no other database field. The Google path never resets failed_logins. It clears g_bind and g_pending and redirects to the stored `next` if it is a relative path (checked again here), else /home.

12. Settings origin. If the sub is already linked to any user, the user goes back to Settings with "already linked to a user" and nothing changes. If this user already has a Google link, Settings shows "Google already linked" and nothing changes. Otherwise the server inserts the user_google_accounts row. No password is asked, the emails need not match, and email_verified is not required. The current session stays as is. A unique violation from a race is handled as "already linked". On success, Settings shows "Google linked".

13. Unlink (POST /settings/google/unlink). This needs a session and a CSRF check. If the user has no link, Settings says "nothing to unlink". If users.password_hash is NULL, the server refuses and tells the user to set a password through the existing reset email (POST /forgot). Otherwise it deletes the user_google_accounts row. Sessions are untouched.

State summary. Redis holds the attempt and the pending record, both with 600s TTLs. PostgreSQL holds the permanent link table (user_id is the primary key and sub is UNIQUE) and the failed_logins and locked_until counters on users. The database unique constraints are the real guard against races.
gaps: The document does not say what the g_bind cookie's Path or lifetime is. It gives the scope and lifetime of g_pending only partly (scoped to /auth/google/confirm, no expiry stated).

The document does not say what is shown or returned after a successful or failed password-confirm POST beyond the cases listed, for example how the 'refuse, nothing linked' message (R5) is displayed to a user who has no session.
The session-bound CSRF mechanism used on the Settings endpoints is not described. The document only says to assume it exists.
The one-time (flash) message mechanism after redirects, and the look of the error page, are not described.
How the server turns a request into 'the signed-in user' at the Settings callback (how it reads the sid cookie and loads the sessions row) is not described.

The document does not describe how a user with no password (Google-created) sees or reaches the Settings page and unlink refusal in the UI. It also does not say how new users get their other required users columns, since only email, password_hash and email_verified_at are mentioned.
